title: Mitral Valve Prolapse
subject: Medicine
summary: A common, often benign, valvular disorder where the mitral leaflets billow into the left atrium during systole, producing a mid‑systolic click and late systolic murmur. It can lead to regurgitation, arrhythmias and, rarely, infective endocarditis.

sections.p: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is defined by systolic displacement of one or both leaflets >2 mm beyond the annular plane, seen on echocardiography. Clinically it presents with a mid‑systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur best heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla.
b: MVP is the most common valvular disease in young women.
It is usually benign but can progress to significant regurgitation or arrhythmias.

t.b: Shows leaflet billowing >2 mm beyond annulus and confirms regurgitation
Detects atrial or ventricular arrhythmias that may be associated with MVP

b: Mild: click only, no murmur or regurgitation
Moderate: click + murmur, mild‑moderate regurgitation
Severe: click + murmur, significant regurgitation, LV enlargement

sections.p: Primary MVP is a connective‑tissue disorder with excess leaflet tissue or weak chordae. Secondary causes include rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, and post‑myocardial‑infarction papillary‑muscle rupture.
b: Primary MVP – familial, often associated with Marfan or Ehlers‑Danlos
Rheumatic fever – common in low‑resource settings
Infective endocarditis – especially with IV drug use or HIV

t.b: Rule out infective endocarditis in patients with fever or new murmur
Shows left‑sided heart enlargement if severe regurgitation

sections.p: Patients report chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea, or a feeling of a fluttering heart. The classic auscultatory finding is a mid‑systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.
b: Chest pain may mimic angina but is usually positional
Palpitations often due to atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia
Dyspnoea occurs when regurgitation is significant

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, a focused history, physical exam, and a basic ECG are first steps. If available, transthoracic echo confirms diagnosis and assesses severity.
b: ECG – look for arrhythmias or left‑atrial enlargement

t.b: Normal: no billowing; MVP: >2 mm billowing; severe regurgitation: >30 mL/beat
Normal: no cardiomegaly; enlarged left heart suggests significant MR

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for signs of heart failure, uncontrolled arrhythmias, or infective endocarditis.
b: Acute pulmonary oedema
Rapidly worsening dyspnoea
New‑onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Fever with new murmur

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. For uncomplicated MVP, reassurance and routine follow‑up are adequate. Symptomatic MR or arrhythmias require medical therapy; severe MR may need surgery.
b: Beta‑blockers – reduce palpitations and improve exercise tolerance
ACE inhibitors/ARBs – used if LV dysfunction develops
Anticoagulation – only if atrial fibrillation or embolic risk

t.b: Avoid in severe asthma or heart block
Avoid in pregnancy or renal failure

sections.p: Annual review with ECG and symptom check. In endemic areas, screen for rheumatic fever and treat streptococcal infections early to prevent secondary MVP.
b: Annual ECG to detect new arrhythmias
Repeat echo every 2–3 years if moderate MR
Penicillin prophylaxis for rheumatic fever

sections.p: Mitral stenosis (fixed opening, diastolic rumble), aortic regurgitation (diastolic decrescendo murmur), and pericardial knock.
b: Mitral stenosis – diastolic rumble, not a click
Aortic regurgitation – diastolic murmur, not systolic

sections.p: In low‑volume echo machines, mild MR may be missed. A normal ECG does not exclude arrhythmias; a Holter may be needed.
b: Echo sensitivity drops below 2 mm billowing
Holter detects paroxysmal arrhythmias missed on 12‑lead ECG

faq.q: Why is a mid‑systolic click heard in MVP?
faq.a: It is the sound of the leaflet or chordae snapping back into place as the valve bulges into the atrium.
Rarely, through ventricular arrhythmias or severe MR leading to heart failure.
Yes, it is often familial and linked to connective‑tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman reports chest pain after exertion and a new heart sound – what is the most likely diagnosis? — MVP (mid‑systolic click + late systolic murmur).
You suspect MVP but the patient has a fever and new murmur – what is the next step? — Obtain blood cultures and start empiric antibiotics for possible endocarditis.
A patient with MVP develops atrial fibrillation – what anticoagulation strategy is appropriate? — Start a vitamin K antagonist or DOAC if no contraindication, considering bleeding risk.
You have a patient with MVP and mild MR – what is the best long‑term management? — Reassurance, beta‑blocker for palpitations, and annual follow‑up.
A patient with MVP presents with acute pulmonary oedema – what is the immediate treatment? — Diuretics, oxygen, and evaluate for severe MR or arrhythmia.
You find a mid‑systolic click but no murmur on exam – what is the significance? — It may indicate mild MVP; repeat exam or echo to confirm.
A patient with MVP is pregnant – which drug class is safest for palpitations? — Beta‑blockers (e.g., labetalol) are preferred over ACE inhibitors.
You observe a late systolic murmur radiating to the axilla – what other condition could mimic this? — Aortic regurgitation (diastolic murmur) or mitral stenosis (diastolic rumble).
